text: Antonio de Padua María Severino López de Santa Anna y Pérez de Lebrón (21 February 1794 – 21 June 1876) was a Mexican general, politician, and caudillo who served as the 8th president of Mexico on multiple occasions between 1833 and 1855 and held the office of vice president from 1837 to 1839. He is widely regarded as a controversial and pivotal figure in 19th-century Mexican politics, often referred to as an "uncrowned monarch" and associated with the "Age of Santa Anna." Born in Xalapa, Veracruz, into a respected Spanish family, he was named after his father, licenciado Antonio López de Santa Anna y Pérez, a lawyer, and his mother, Manuela Pérez de Lebrón y Cortés. His family prospered in Veracruz, where the merchant class dominated politics; his paternal uncle, Ángel López de Santa Anna, was a public clerk who became disgruntled when barred from moving to Mexico City due to the Spanish crown’s preference for peninsular-born Spaniards. Santa Anna’s mother supported his military career over his father’s preference for commerce, and her relationship with the intendant of Veracruz secured his early military appointment. The family had seven children, including four sisters and two brothers, with Santa Anna being close to his sister Francisca and brother Manuel, who also joined the army. His origins in Veracruz gave him immunity from yellow fever, a significant advantage in military campaigns, and contributed to his rise as a provincial leader. He began his military career in 1810 at age 16 with the Fijo de Veracruz regiment, fought against insurgents during the Mexican War of Independence, and was wounded in 1811. He later served in Texas and earned recognition for bravery at the Battle of Medina. When Agustín de Iturbide switched sides in 1821 to support independence, Santa Anna joined him, was granted command of Veracruz, and later rebelled against Iturbide in 1822, claiming the dissolution of the Constituent Congress as justification. He then participated in the Plan of Casa Mata, which led to the end of the First Mexican Empire and the establishment of a republic. In 1823, he was sent to Yucatán, where he planned an invasion of Cuba but abandoned it when Spanish reinforcements arrived. After the 1828 election, when conservative Manuel Gómez Pedraza won, Santa Anna rebelled, nullified the results, and expelled Spanish nationals, leading to Gómez Pedraza’s resignation and the rise of Guerrero. In 1829, Santa Anna defeated a Spanish invasion at Tampico, earning the title "Victor of Tampico" and "Savior of the Patria," and styled himself the "Napoleon of the West." When Vice President Anastasio Bustamante overthrew Guerrero in 1829, Santa Anna seized Veracruz’s customs revenues and declared rebellion, forcing Bustamante’s cabinet to resign and leading to new elections in 1833. Santa Anna was elected president on 1 April 1833, but he was not interested in governing and is described as an "absentee president," with Vice President Valentín Gómez Farías managing day-to-day affairs. Gómez Farías implemented liberal reforms, including abolishing tithing, seizing church property, closing the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico, and secularizing Franciscan missions in Alta California. These actions provoked strong opposition from the church and army, leading to the Plan of Cuernavaca, which called for the repeal of the Ley del Caso, the removal of reform supporters, and the recognition of Santa Anna as the sole authority. As opposition grew, Santa Anna returned to the presidency, and Gómez Farías resigned, marking a shift from a federalist republic to a unitary central republic. Historians debate the number of his presidencies: Will Fowler cites six, the Texas State Historical Association claims five, Alexander Dawson and the University of Texas Libraries state eleven, though the latter notes he was only president for six years due to short terms. Santa Anna is viewed negatively in Mexican history, often ranked as "the principal inhabitant even today of Mexico's black pantheon of those who failed the nation," and considered one of the most unpopular and controversial Mexican presidents. After being overthrown and exiled in 1855 through the Plan of Ayutla, he faded from prominence during the Reform War, the Second French Intervention, and the establishment of the Second Mexican Empire. An elderly Santa Anna was allowed to return in 1874 by President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada and died in relative obscurity in 1876. He is best known in the United States for his roles in the Texas Revolution and the Mexican–American War, where his leadership prolonged the conflict and contributed to the Mexican Cession and the Gadsden Purchase in 1853. His intermittent rule from 1832 to 1853 saw the loss of Texas, military failures, and territorial concessions. Historian Alexander Dawson notes that Santa Anna switched sides between the Liberal and Conservative Parties, playing a key role in both discarding and restoring the liberal Constitution of 1824. He is remembered as a populist caudillo who used military power to dissolve Congress and referred to himself as "His Most Serene Highness."

Santa Anna's influence was marked by secret political maneuvers involving Masonic lodges; he declared void the laws passed by Congress and local legislatures in favor of reforms, requested protection from Santa Anna to implement his plan and recognize him as the sole authority, removed deputies and officials enforcing reform laws and decrees, and provided military support to Gómez Farías to carry out the reforms. As public opinion turned against the reforms, Santa Anna returned to the presidency and Gómez Farías resigned, setting the stage for conservatives to transform Mexico from a federalist republic into a unitary central republic. Conservatives viewed Gómez Farías's liberal reforms as radical and a threat to elite power; Santa Anna's initial support for the reforms—followed by a more extensive one in 1855—may have been a test of liberalism, allowing him plausible deniability while monitoring reactions to attacks on army and church privileges and the confiscation of church wealth. In May 1834, Santa Anna ordered the disarmament of civic militias and urged Congress to abolish the controversial Ley del Caso; on 12 June, he dissolved Congress and announced the Plan of Cuernavaca, establishing a new Catholic, centralist, and conservative government. In exchange for preserving church and army privileges, the church agreed to provide a monthly donation of 30,000–40,000 pesos, which the santanistas succeeded in achieving, forcing the church to financially support the republic. On 4 January 1835, Santa Anna returned to his hacienda, appointing Miguel Barragán as acting president, and replaced the 1824 constitution with the "Siete Leyes" ("The Seven Laws"). He did not participate in the conservative efforts to replace the federalist constitution with a unitary system, remaining uneasy with their political direction, and was not present during any deliberations that led to the abolition of the federalist charter or the creation of the 1836 Constitution. Several states rebelled, including Alta California, Nuevo México, Tabasco, Sonora, Coahuila y Tejas, San Luis Potosí, Querétaro, Durango, Guanajuato, Michoacán, Yucatán, Jalisco, Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, and Zacatecas, with some forming independent governments such as the Republic of the Rio Grande, the Republic of Yucatán, and the Republic of Texas; resistance was fueled by Santa Anna's reprisals against defeated enemies. The Zacatecas militia, led by Francisco García Salinas and armed with .753 caliber British 'Brown Bess' muskets and Baker .61 rifles, was defeated by Santa Anna's "Army of Operations" on 12 May 1835, resulting in nearly 3,000 prisoners and a 48-hour looting of Zacatecas City. After conquering Zacatecas, Santa Anna planned to move to Coahuila y Tejas to suppress the rebellion supported by U.S. settlers. In 1835, Santa Anna repealed the Mexican constitution, citing that American settlers in Texas were not paying taxes or tariffs because they did not receive government services, and thus new settlers were barred from Texas, a response to U.S. attempts to purchase the territory. Late in 1835, the Texas Department of Coahuila y Tejas rebelled and declared independence on 2 March 1836, with the northeastern region settled by American immigrants, including those from Moses Austin's party, who had been accepted by Spanish authorities for defense against foreign threats, though Mexico had declared independence from Spain before Austin's death. Santa Anna marched north to reassert control over Texas with brutal force, facing severe logistical challenges including cold weather, inadequate clothing, food shortages, poor medical supplies, and a lack of horses, mules, cattle, and wagons, with hostile Indigenous groups attacking stragglers and waterborne diseases spreading rapidly. The army's officers were largely incompetent, and the rigid hierarchy prevented Santa Anna from being informed of these problems. At the Battle of the Alamo on 6 March 1836, Santa Anna's forces killed 189 Texan defenders, and at the Goliad Massacre on 27 March 1836, over 342 Texan prisoners were executed; Santa Anna claimed that killing the Alamo defenders was necessary because Texan commander William B. Travis was disrespectful to him and that sparing them would have allowed Sam Houston to gain power threatening Santa Anna. The Mexican victory at the Alamo provided time for Houston and his forces to gain experience and weaponry. Despite Houston's poor command, Texas forces completely defeated Santa Anna's larger army at the Battle of San Jacinto on 21 April 1836. The day after, James Austin Sylvester captured Santa Anna near a marsh; he had hastily dressed in a dead Mexican dragoon's uniform but was quickly recognized. After three weeks in captivity, Texas President David G. Burnet and Santa Anna signed the Treaties of Velasco, in which Santa Anna acknowledged the full, entire, and perfect independence of the Republic of Texas, in exchange for guarantees of his safety and transport to Veracruz. In Mexico City, a new government declared the treaties null and void. Poinsett criticized Santa Anna, saying he had no sympathy for him now after having once been a passionate advocate of liberty, to which Santa Anna replied that he had once supported liberty with sincerity but soon realized its folly, stating that Mexico's people were unenlightened and under the influence of Catholic clergy, making despotism a proper and wise government. After time in exile and meeting U.S. President Andrew Jackson in 1837, Santa Anna was allowed to return to Mexico and retired to his hacienda in Veracruz, where he wrote a manifesto reflecting on his decisions. In 1838, Santa Anna found redemption after Mexico rejected demands for financial compensation for losses, prompting France to launch the Pastry War by landing forces in Veracruz. The Mexican government gave Santa Anna control of the army and ordered him to defend the nation; he engaged the French at Veracruz, retreated after a failed assault, and sustained injuries to his left leg and hand, requiring amputation of much of his leg, which he buried with full military honors. Despite Mexico's eventual capitulation, Santa Anna used his war service and sacrifice to re-enter politics. When Bustamante's presidency collapsed, supporters asked Santa Anna to take control of the provisional government, and he became president for the fifth time, ruling a nation with an empty treasury, facing rebellion led by Generals José de Urrea and José Antonio Mexía, which he crushed in Puebla. Santa Anna ruled more dictatorially, banning anti-Santanista newspapers and imprisoning dissidents. In 1842, he launched a military expedition into Texas, inflicting casualties without political gain, but it persuaded Texans of the potential benefits of annexation by the United States. After the 1842 elections, when a new Congress opposed his rule, Santa Anna attempted to restore the treasury by raising taxes, leading several states to withdraw from the central government, with Yucatán and Laredo declaring independence. With growing resentment, Santa Anna stepped down and fled Mexico City in December 1844; his buried leg was dug up by a mob and dragged through the streets until nothing remained. Fearing for his life, he tried to evade capture but was apprehended in January 1845 by Native Americans near Xico, turned over to authorities, and imprisoned; his life was spared, and he was exiled to Cuba. In 1846, following American victories at Palo Alto and Resaca de la Palma in the Mexican-American War, President Mariano Paredes was removed, and the new government sought to restore the 1824 constitution, with Santa Anna again assuming the presidency. Santa Anna, having been in exile for only a year, returned to Mexico on 6 August 1846, two days after Paredes' removal, stating he had no ambition for the presidency but would use his military experience in the conflict with the U.S. U.S. President James K. Polk sought to acquire northern territory by purchase or force, but Mexico refused. Polk sent agents to secretly meet with exiled Santa Anna, believing they had secured a promise for him to lift a blockade and broker a deal; however, upon returning to Mexico with an army, Santa Anna reneged and took up arms against the U.S. invasion. With no quick resolution, Polk authorized an invasion to take Mexico City, redirecting most of General Zachary Taylor's troops to General Winfield Scott's army. Santa Anna mobilized troops and artillery and rapidly marched north; his forces outnumbered Taylor's, but were exhausted, ill-clothed, hungry, and poorly equipped when they clashed at the Battle of Buena Vista on 22–23 February 1847. After two days of hard fighting, Santa Anna withdrew just as victory was imminent, taking war trophies such as cannons and battle flags. When Scott's army landed at Veracruz, Santa Anna quickly moved south to defend the capital. He set defenses at Cerro Gordo, but U.S. forces outflanked him and defeated his army. The path to Mexico City was clear; Santa Anna aimed to protect the capital and waged defensive warfare, placing strong defenses at El Peñon, which Scott avoided. Battles at Contreras, Churubusco, and Molino del Rey were lost; at Contreras, General Gabriel Valencia, a political and military rival of Santa Anna, disobeyed his orders and was routed. The Battle for Mexico City and the Battle of Chapultepec were hard-fought losses, and American forces captured the capital. Despite his tactical flaws and political ambition, Santa Anna was committed to fighting to the end, prolonging the war by at least a year and denying Polk's dream of a short war. One of Santa Anna's most personal and humiliating incidents was the capture during the Battle of Cerro Gordo of his prosthetic cork leg, which remains a war trophy in the Illinois State Military Museum and is no longer on display; a second leg, a peg, was captured by the 4th Illinois and used as a baseball bat, displayed at the home of Illinois Governor Richard J. Oglesby in Decatur; a replacement leg is displayed at the Museo Nacional de Historia in Mexico City. The prosthetic leg later influenced international politics; as U.S.-Mexico relations improved before World War II, Illinois considered returning the leg, and in 1942 a bill was introduced in the state legislature, with the Association of Limb Manufacturers wanting to participate in the repatriation. The state passed a non-binding resolution to return the leg, but the National Guard denied the transfer; as of 2025, the leg remains in the Illinois State Military Museum in Springfield. Following Mexico's defeat in 1848, Santa Anna went into exile in Kingston, Jamaica, then moved to Turbaco in New Granada (now Colombia). In April 1853, conservatives who had overthrown a weak liberal government under the Plan de Hospicio, drawn up by clerics in the cathedral chapter of Guadalajara, invited him to return to Mexico. Santa Anna was elected president on 17 March 1853; he honored his promises to the church by revoking a decree denying protection for monastic vows, a reform from 20 years earlier by Gómez Farías. The Jesuits, expelled from Spanish realms in 1767, were allowed to return to Mexico to educate poorer classes, and much of their property, confiscated and sold by the crown, was restored. Although he gave himself exalted titles, including "Most Serene Highness" and the full title "Hero [benemérito] of the nation, General of Division, Grand Master of the National and Distinguished Order of Guadalupe, Grand Cross of the Royal and Distinguished Spanish Order of Carlos III, and President of the Mexican Republic," his administration was no more successful than previous ones, relying on loans from moneylenders and support from conservative elites, the church, and the army. A major miscalculation was Santa Anna's sale of territory to the U.S. in the Gadsden Purchase, where the land in northwest Mexico (La Mesilla) was easier for building a transcontinental railway in the U.S. The purchase money was supposed to go to Mexico's treasury, but Santa Anna wanted immediate access to funds and bargained with American bankers for immediate cash, while they gained rights to future revenue. The deal netted Mexico only $250,000 against $650,000 in credit to the bankers, with James Gadsden believing the amount was likely higher. A group of liberals, including Alvarez, Benito Juárez, and Ignacio Comonfort, overthrew Santa Anna under the Plan of Ayutla in 1855, and he went into exile once again. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the United States paid.

Santa Anna made a major miscalculation by selling territory to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase, which involved land in northwest Mexico known as La Mesilla. This area was considered easier for building a transcontinental railway in the U.S., and the purchase money was intended to benefit Mexico’s empty treasury. However, Santa Anna sought immediate access to funds and negotiated with American bankers to receive cash upfront, with the bankers gaining rights to future revenue. The deal resulted in Mexico receiving only $250,000 against a credit of $650,000 going to the bankers, a sum James Gadsden believed was likely much higher. A group of liberal leaders, including Alvarez, Benito Juárez, and Ignacio Comonfort, overthrew Santa Anna under the Plan of Ayutla, leading to his exile in 1855. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the United States paid Mexico $15 million for the land, known as the Mexican Cession. Santa Anna married twice: first in 1825 to Inés García, daughter of wealthy Spanish parents in Veracruz, with whom he had four children—María de Guadalupe, María del Carmen, Manuel, and Antonio López de Santa Anna y García. His family background was of modest means, but his creole lineage and the dowry from Inés allowed him to purchase his first hacienda, Manga de Clavo, in Veracruz. The first Spanish ambassador to Mexico, Fanny Calderón de la Barca, visited Inés at Manga de Clavo and noted the hospitality, including a breakfast where Inés offered her a cigar and others followed suit. Two months after Inés’ death in 1844, Santa Anna married 16-year-old María de los Dolores de Tosta; they rarely lived together, with De Tosta residing in Mexico City and Santa Anna traveling for political and military duties. They had no children, and biographer Will Fowler speculated the marriage was either platonic or that De Tosta was infertile. Several women claimed to have borne Santa Anna natural children; in his will, he acknowledged and provided for four—Paula, María de la Merced, Petra, and José López de Santa Anna—and biographers have identified three more: Pedro López de Santa Anna, Ángel and Augustina Rosa López de Santa Anna. From 1855 to 1874, Santa Anna lived in exile in Cuba, the United States, Colombia, and Saint Thomas, leaving Mexico due to his unpopularity after his defeat in 1848. During exile, he engaged in gambling and business ventures, and was a passionate fan of cockfighting, maintaining many roosters for competitions. In the 1850s, he traveled to New York City with a shipment of chicle, intending to sell it for carriage wheels, but failed to convince U.S. manufacturers of its usefulness in tires. Although he introduced chewing gum to the U.S., he did not profit from it. Thomas Adams, assigned to assist Santa Anna, experimented with chicle and, though his attempts to use it as rubber failed, helped found the chewing gum industry with a product called "chiclets." In 1865, Santa Anna tried to return to Mexico to serve during the French invasion, but was refused by Juárez. That year, a schooner owned by Gilbert Thompson, son-in-law of Daniel Tompkins, brought him to Staten Island, where he attempted to raise funds for an army to retake Mexico City. In 1874, Santa Anna returned to Mexico under a general amnesty issued by President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, having become crippled and nearly blind from cataracts. He died at his home in Mexico City on 21 June 1876 at age 82 and was buried with full military honors in a glass coffin at Panteón del Tepeyac Cemetery. Santa Anna was highly controversial, with Will Fowler describing him as a liberal, Republican, army man, hero, revolutionary, and regional strongman, but never a politician, who presented himself as a mediator against party politics and was more willing to lead armies than govern. Historian Gates Brown considers Santa Anna one of history’s worst military leaders due to his errors in two wars that cost Mexico significant territory. During the Texas Revolution, Santa Anna attacked the Alamo after knowing the defenders would not be reinforced, despite having time to build a logistical base at San Antonio. He lost more men than the defenders, sacrificing a third of his force, and his subsequent executions at the Alamo and Goliad fueled rebellion. He also mistakenly believed General Houston would not attack with a smaller, tired force, contributing to his defeat at San Jacinto. In the Mexican-American War, Santa Anna marched newly recruited and inexperienced troops across 385 kilometers (239 miles) of desert in winter without resupplying, leading to heavy Mexican casualties at Buena Vista. At Cerro Gordo, he dismissed advice from officer Manuel Robles Pezuela to reinforce Atalaya hill, believing the terrain made it unnecessary; the U.S. attack and flanking maneuver destroyed Mexico’s chance to stop General Winfield Scott’s advance on Mexico City. Santa Anna became prominent in Tejano folk memory due to his role in the Texas Revolution and the Alamo. Texas educators, writers, and officials portrayed him as the central antagonist in Texas’ independence narrative, contributing to an exaggerated view of his personal influence and a symbolic representation of Mexican autocracy, rather than a complex figure navigating internal Mexican instability. Stephen Oleszek argues that Santa Anna’s rise as a Texas folk legend is tied to myth-making around the Alamo, where he was depicted as a symbol of despotism while Alamo defenders like William B. Travis and James Bowie were portrayed as heroes, reinforcing a hero-villain dichotomy to unify Anglo-Americans and justify the Texas Revolution. This narrative has been embedded in textbooks, media, and the slogan "Remember the Alamo!" More recent works, such as Santa Anna in Texas: A Mexican American Viewpoint, show that Mexican perspectives on Santa Anna were divided and often did not align with the villainous Texan narrative. In the 21st century, historians emphasize the distinction between cultural memory and historical reality, noting that Santa Anna’s reputation evolved from a historical figure into a legend centered on the Battle of the Alamo.
